newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: World Insurance Network gives some price details.
newsitem.headline: World Insurance Network gives some price details.

text.p: Price details of the World Insurance Network (WIN) were given to an insurance conference on Wednesday, but delegates still harbour suspicions about how it will work.
WIN is an electronic information system being developed by the four top insurance brokers -- J&H Marsh & McLennan, Aon, Sedgwick and Willis Corroon. It is due for launch on July 1.
Sales manager Tony Briggs told the London International Insurance and Reinsurance Association (LIRMA) seminar in Dublin there will be a range of fees.

"The up front joining fee will be half the annual fee, and the annual fee will be determined by the size of the subscribing company measured by its total non-life gross written premiums (GWP)," Briggs said.
The maximum joining fee will be $150,000 and the minimum will be $10,000 for a company with $150 million GWP, Briggs told Reuters.

"There will be a connection fee of around 2,000 pounds and a monthly access fee of between one and two thousand pounds. The hardware will cost around 5,000 pounds and there will be a monthly service charge of around 2,000," he said.
Briggs said he could not reveal the traffic charge which would apply to each transaction for commercial sensitivity reasons.

Pilot tests will commence on April 21, 1997, and involve six companies -- U.S. insurance giant Cigna, Commercial Union and Royal & Sun Alliance in the UK, Italy's Generali, Gerling in Germany and X.L. in Bermuda.
The pilot is scheduled to end during May prior to the launch date on July 1, 1997, he said.
He added that WIN would be rolled out to Asia Pacific companies at the end of 1997, and would open offices in the U.S. later in the year.
Additional information services will be available on the system from Reuters and Sedgwick.
Some delegates at the conference said they were concerned about the effect WIN would have on other electronic systems developed at high cost in different parts of the market.

Mike Hannan, chief executive of the London Processing Centre, said, "I would prefer to see WIN as a front end that links into the existing systems in the market which companies have invested in, rather than subsuming them."
Briggs replied, "Inevitably, there will be some conflicts as we go ahead, but we will not seek them."
Afterwards Briggs told Reuters he had learned a lot from the slightly cynical response of some delegates.
"We clearly still have to sell this to them. That will be easier when we have something to show," he said.
